sections.heading: 1 · The Physics You Need First
bullets: Power = Voltage × Current (P = V·I), and wires waste power as heat proportional to current squared (I²R). Moving the same power at higher voltage means less current, less copper, and a quarter of the losses every time voltage doubles. This is why solar plants run strings at 1,500 V DC and why plant voltages keep climbing.

The grid runs on AC (alternating current — cheap to change voltage with transformers); solar panels and batteries produce/consume DC (direct current). The INVERTER — the machine that turns DC into grid-synchronized AC — is therefore the single most important box in renewable energy, and it's the product this company is built on.

A solar cell is a semiconductor sandwich (a silicon p-n junction): photons knock electrons loose, the junction's electric field sweeps them one way, and you get DC current. One cell makes ~0.7 V, so panels wire ~60–140 cells in series, and plants wire panels into STRINGS of 20–30 to reach ~1,500 V.

A panel's power output depends on sunlight, temperature, and the electrical load you present to it. There is one operating point that extracts maximum power at any moment — MPPT (maximum power point tracking) is the algorithm that continuously finds it. More independent MPPT channels = less energy lost when parts of a plant are shaded, dusty, or mismatched.

Batteries store energy chemically. Grid storage overwhelmingly uses LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cells — less energy-dense than the cells in your phone but far safer and longer-lived (10,000+ cycles). Key vocabulary: Ah (amp-hours, cell capacity), C-rate (charge/discharge speed relative to capacity — 0.5C empties in 2 hours), cycle life (full charge-discharge cycles before capacity fades to ~80%).

Modern converters chop current with semiconductor switches at tens of kilohertz. New wide-bandgap semiconductors — especially silicon carbide (SiC) — switch faster with lower losses than plain silicon, which is why the newest power conversion systems are smaller, cooler, and push 99%+ efficiency.

sections.heading: 2 · How a Solar + Storage Plant Works Today
bullets: Follow the electrons in a utility solar plant: panels → series strings (~1,500 V DC) → inverters (DC → 3-phase AC at several hundred volts) → medium-voltage transformer (steps up to 10–35 kV) → substation (steps up again to high voltage) → grid. Everything a plant buys besides the panels — cabling, combiners, inverters, transformers — is called BOS (balance of system).

Two inverter philosophies compete. STRING inverters: many smaller units (~250–500 kW) spread through the plant, each with its own MPPTs — fine-grained shade/mismatch handling, and one failure loses only a sliver of the plant. CENTRAL inverters: a few multi-MW machines — cheaper per watt but coarse control and a big single point of failure. Modular designs try to capture both advantages: central-class blocks assembled from swappable sub-modules.

Storage plugs into this picture as containerized batteries plus a PCS (power conversion system — a bidirectional inverter that charges and discharges the battery). A modern grid-scale unit packs battery racks, liquid cooling, fire protection, and often the PCS into one 20-foot shipping container; plants chain containers into 'blocks' and blocks into GWh-scale plants.

Why liquid cooling took over: battery cells age fast when hot and, worse, unevenly aged cells drift apart in behavior. Liquid plates hold every cell within a couple of degrees of its neighbors, extending life and allowing more energy in the same box. Thermal runaway (a cell overheating into self-sustaining reaction) is the failure mode all the fire engineering exists to contain.

What storage is FOR: shifting solar from midday (when it's abundant and cheap) to evening (when it's scarce and expensive), smoothing ramps, providing frequency response, and capacity — being paid to be available. Duration matters: a '4-hour' system has 4 MWh of energy per MW of power. Longer durations are winning as solar penetration rises.

The grid runs at a precise frequency (50/60 Hz) held steady historically by the spinning mass of coal/gas/hydro turbines — physical inertia that resists sudden change. As those retire, grids dominated by inverters lose that stabilizer. This is the problem 'grid-forming' inverters exist to solve (Section 3), and it's why the term keeps appearing in every modern tender.

sections.heading: 3 · Sungrow's Core Products, Mapped Into That System
bullets: SG-HX UTILITY STRING INVERTERS (SG350HX, new SG510HX/SG465HX): the plant's DC→AC workhorses. The SG350HX gives 352 kVA with up to 16 MPPT channels at 99% peak efficiency; the newest generation raises output to ~465–510 kW and the AC side to 1,000 V — higher voltage, less current, less copper (Section 1 physics) — letting one subarray reach ~9.8 MW. What they displace: older central-only designs and lower-voltage string fleets that need more units and more cabling per MW.

'1+X' MODULAR INVERTER (2.0: 800 kW modules, paralleling up to 9.6 MW): the string-vs-central compromise resolved — central-inverter economics built from swappable 800 kW modules, so a failure means replacing one module, not craning out a multi-MW machine. Finer 'power granularity' also lets plant designers right-size blocks instead of rounding up to a big central unit's size.

POWERTITAN UTILITY BESS: the storage flagship. PowerTitan 2.0 packs 5 MWh + a 2.5 MW PCS into one 20-ft container as an 'AC block' — battery and inverter pre-integrated and pre-tested at the factory, so the site gets plug-together AC units instead of a field-engineered DC yard. PowerTitan 3.0 (2025) jumps to a giant 684 Ah LFP cell (bigger cells = fewer parts and welds per MWh), a silicon-carbide PCS, and up to 12.5 MWh per container — with a 4-hour European variant (7.14 MWh / 1.78 MW) tuned to what European markets actually buy.

GRID-FORMING vs GRID-FOLLOWING — the concept that wins modern tenders: a grid-FOLLOWING inverter measures the grid's existing voltage waveform and injects current in sync with it (it needs a healthy grid to lean on); a grid-FORMING inverter creates its own voltage waveform and behaves like a virtual generator — contributing synthetic inertia, riding through disturbances, even black-starting a dead grid. Sungrow's 'Stem Cell' grid-forming control runs across its storage, PV, and wind lines; its 7.8 GWh Saudi fleet is described as the world's largest grid-forming storage plant.

SAFETY AS A SPEC: because thermal runaway is storage's existential risk, vendors now compete on proof. Sungrow ran the industry's largest burn tests — deliberately igniting fully charged multi-container systems (20 MWh in the 2024 test) with fire suppression disabled, third-party witnessed, to demonstrate a burning container doesn't cascade to its neighbors. Insurers, permitting authorities, and buyers treat this evidence as a purchasing criterion.

STORAGE PCS: the bidirectional inverter inside every BESS. Doing it in-house with SiC (99%+ conversion efficiency) matters twice — every conversion loss is paid on BOTH charge and discharge, so PCS efficiency compounds into the round-trip figure (~92% on PowerTitan 3.0) that determines how much bought energy comes back out as sold energy.

sections.heading: 4 · The Rest of the Portfolio, Same Physics
bullets: POWERSTACK (C&I storage): the PowerTitan idea shrunk to factory/commercial scale — 257–514 kWh cabinets with a 125 kW PCS, liquid cooling, and integrated EMS/BMS. Businesses use them to cut peak-demand charges, self-consume rooftop solar, and back up operations. Same cell chemistry, same thermal logic, smaller box.

RESIDENTIAL HYBRIDS + BATTERIES: a hybrid inverter is one box handling rooftop PV, a home battery, and backup — one DC→AC stage shared by panels and battery instead of two separate systems. Sungrow's SH ranges (3–25 kW) pair with stackable 3.2 or 5 kWh LFP modules (up to 160 kWh in parallel), switching a home to backup power in under 10 ms — faster than most electronics notice.

EV CHARGING: a DC fast charger is a rectifier bank pointed at cars — Sungrow builds 40 kW modules (>97% efficient) and parallels them up to 480 kW, the same modular N+ philosophy as its inverters. Bundled as PV + storage + charging ('Beyond Charging'): storage buffers the grid connection so a site can offer megawatt-class charging without a megawatt-class utility feed.

HYDROGEN ELECTROLYZERS: electrolysis runs a fuel cell in reverse — DC current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. The two technologies: ALKALINE (ALK — cheap, huge, up to 2,000 Nm³/h units, likes steady power) and PEM (compact, fast-responding, follows fluctuating solar/wind, 300 Nm³/h units). The overlooked fact: an electrolyzer plant is largely a giant rectifier — the DC power supply is core Sungrow competence, which is why an inverter company credibly sells hydrogen equipment, including hybrid ALK+PEM plants tuned to variable renewables.

FLOATING PV: solar on reservoirs and mining pits — saves land, cuts water evaporation, and cooler panels perform better. The hard engineering isn't the panel, it's the marine part: floats that survive decades of UV and waves, and anchoring/mooring that handles wind loads and water-level swings (Sungrow FPV anchored a project in 100 m deep water; its design methodology is DNV-verified).

WIND CONVERTERS: a wind turbine's rotor speed varies with the wind, so its raw AC output is grid-unusable until a converter (AC→DC→AC) decouples the generator from the grid — the same power-electronics core again. Sungrow supplies converters from 1.5 to 26 MW-class turbines to wind OEMs.

iSOLARCLOUD (digital layer): fleet monitoring, remote configuration, and AI fault diagnosis for 1M+ users across 150+ countries — plus the EMS that decides when storage charges and discharges. Strategically, it's the recurring relationship layered over every hardware sale: the hardware is bought once; the platform is used daily.

sections.heading: 5 · Industry Map — Who Buys, Who Competes, Why It Matters
bullets: WHO BUYS: project developers and IPPs (independent power producers) who build and own plants; EPC contractors (engineering-procurement-construction) who build them; utilities; and at small scale, installers buying through distributors. Utility deals are direct and huge — single orders now reach multiple GWh (7.8 GWh Saudi Arabia, 7.5 GWh Abu Dhabi) — while residential/C&I flows through distribution partners.

WHO COMPETES — inverters: Sungrow and Huawei are the global duopoly (together >55% of the market), with SMA, Fronius, GoodWe, and others behind. Competition runs on efficiency, MPPT granularity, grid-code features (grid-forming now), harsh-climate reliability, and bankability — whether lenders trust the vendor to exist for the plant's 25-year life.

WHO COMPETES — storage: Tesla (Megapack, US manufacturing advantage), CATL (the world's biggest cell maker moving up into systems), BYD, and integrators like Fluence and Wärtsilä. Sungrow's angle: it builds the PCS/inverter side in-house (cell makers can't), pre-integrates AC blocks, leads on deployed grid-forming, and burn-tests at full scale. Rankings flipped in 2025–26: Sungrow took Wood Mackenzie's #1 BESS integrator spot from Tesla — the first time both the storage and inverter crowns sat with one company.

WHY THE ECONOMICS MATTER: solar is the cheapest electricity in history in good locations, but it peaks at noon — storage converts cheap midday energy into valuable evening energy, and the spread pays for the battery. Battery costs keep falling, so each year storage pencils in more markets; that's why storage revenue overtook inverter revenue as this industry's growth engine.

THE GRID-FORMING PRIZE: as renewables displace spinning turbines, the scarce product stops being energy and becomes STABILITY — inertia, frequency response, black-start. Grids (Australia, UK, Iberia, the Gulf) increasingly require or pay extra for grid-forming capability, converting an engineering feature directly into revenue and tender wins.

THE ONE-SENTENCE SYNTHESIS: one core competence — high-efficiency conversion between DC and AC plus the control software around it — sold as solar inverters, storage systems, EV chargers, electrolyzer power supplies, wind converters, and a monitoring cloud, into a grid that is being rebuilt around exactly that competence.

flashcards.q: Why do solar plants run strings at 1,500 V DC instead of lower voltages?
flashcards.a: P = V·I and losses = I²R: at higher voltage the same power flows with less current, so wiring losses shrink with the square of the reduction and thinner (cheaper) copper suffices. Higher string voltage also means fewer parallel circuits and less BOS hardware per MW. The same logic drives the new AC-1,000 V inverter generation.

flashcards.q: What does an inverter do, and why is it the central product of renewable energy?
flashcards.a: It converts DC (what panels and batteries produce) into AC synchronized with the grid (what the power system runs on). Every solar plant, battery, EV charger, and wind turbine needs this conversion — so the vendor of the conversion box sits at the choke point of the entire energy transition.

flashcards.q: What is MPPT and why do more MPPT channels capture more energy?
flashcards.a: Maximum power point tracking — an algorithm that continuously adjusts the electrical operating point to extract the most power available from a panel string at that moment. Each independent channel optimizes its own strings, so shading, soiling, or mismatch in one area doesn't drag down the rest of the array.

flashcards.q: String inverter vs central inverter vs modular ('1+X') — what's the trade-off?
flashcards.a: String: many small units, fine MPPT granularity, small failure impact, but more units to install. Central: few multi-MW machines, cheapest per watt, but coarse control and big single points of failure. Modular: a central-class block built from swappable sub-modules (e.g. 800 kW × up to 12) — central economics with module-level serviceability and right-sized blocks.

flashcards.q: What is an 'AC block' in grid-scale storage and why did the industry adopt it?
flashcards.a: A container that integrates battery racks AND the PCS (bidirectional inverter), factory-built and tested, delivering plug-together AC units to site. It replaces field-engineered DC yards — faster installation, fewer site interfaces, and higher system round-trip efficiency because the DC-side integration is optimized in the factory.

flashcards.q: Why is LFP chemistry standard for grid storage, and why are cells getting huge (314 Ah → 684 Ah)?
flashcards.a: LFP (lithium iron phosphate) trades energy density for safety (much harder to ignite) and long cycle life (10,000+ cycles) — exactly what a 20-year stationary asset needs. Bigger cells mean fewer cells, welds, and connections per MWh — lower cost and fewer failure points — provided thermal design keeps the larger cell's interior cool.

flashcards.q: What is thermal runaway and how do storage vendors prove they can contain it?
flashcards.a: A failing cell overheating into a self-sustaining exothermic reaction that can cascade to neighbors — storage's existential risk. Vendors now run full-scale burn tests: igniting fully charged containers with suppression disabled, third-party witnessed, to prove fire doesn't propagate container-to-container. Test evidence has become a purchasing and permitting criterion.

flashcards.q: Grid-forming vs grid-following inverter — what's the difference and why does it matter now?
flashcards.a: Grid-following injects current in sync with a voltage waveform the grid already provides — it needs a healthy grid to lean on. Grid-forming generates its own voltage waveform like a virtual generator: synthetic inertia, disturbance ride-through, black-start. As spinning turbines retire, grids lose physical inertia, so tenders increasingly require — and pay extra for — grid-forming capability.

flashcards.q: Why does PCS efficiency matter twice in storage economics?
flashcards.a: Every conversion loss is paid on both charge AND discharge, so PCS losses compound into the round-trip efficiency — the fraction of bought energy that comes back out as sellable energy (~92% on the latest systems). A single point of PCS efficiency is worth real revenue over thousands of cycles, which is why SiC-based 99%+ PCS designs are a selling point.

flashcards.q: Why is liquid cooling now standard in battery containers?
flashcards.a: Cells age faster when hot and drift apart when unevenly heated — divergent cells limit the whole pack. Liquid plates hold cell-to-cell temperature spread to a couple of degrees, extending life, enabling denser packing, and cutting the auxiliary (cooling) energy the plant itself burns.

flashcards.q: What is a hybrid inverter in a home solar system?
flashcards.a: One box that manages rooftop PV, a battery, and backup through a shared DC→AC stage — instead of separate solar and battery inverters. It can island the home during an outage (switchover in ~10 ms) and optimize self-consumption: store midday solar, use it in the evening.

flashcards.q: What does storage 'duration' mean, and why are 4-hour systems winning?
flashcards.a: Duration = energy ÷ power (MWh per MW): a 4-hour system discharges at full power for 4 hours. As solar floods midday markets, the value shifts to carrying energy into the evening peak — which needs longer durations. That's why vendors now ship duration-optimized variants (more MWh, less MW per container) for markets like Europe.

flashcards.q: ALK vs PEM electrolyzers — and why can an inverter company credibly sell hydrogen equipment?
flashcards.a: Alkaline (ALK): cheap, very large (2,000 Nm³/h class), prefers steady power. PEM: compact, fast-responding, follows fluctuating renewables (300 Nm³/h class); hybrid plants combine both. An electrolyzer plant is largely a giant DC power supply (rectifier) — core power-electronics competence — so the conversion vendor already builds the hardest part.

flashcards.q: What's technically hard about floating PV — the panels or something else?
flashcards.a: The marine engineering: floats that survive decades of UV, waves, and temperature swings, and anchoring/mooring that handles wind loads, water-level changes, and difficult bottoms (including 100 m deep water). The panels are standard; the float-and-anchor system design is the differentiating product.

flashcards.q: Why does a wind turbine need a power converter at all?
flashcards.a: Rotor speed varies with the wind, so the generator's raw AC varies in frequency and can't feed a fixed-frequency grid. The converter rectifies it to DC and re-synthesizes clean grid-frequency AC, decoupling the generator from the grid — same core electronics as a solar inverter, pointed at a different energy source.
